panacea

/pan-uh-SEE-uh/ - the stress falls on SEE · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Panacea means a remedy for all ills or difficulties.

Every decade crowns a new kitchen panacea — vinegar, then kale, now fermented everything — and every decade the ailments outlast the trend.

Example

When the star quarterback transferred in, half the town saw him as a panacea for the losing streak. The coach kept repeating that one arm could not block, kick, or cover; the line still leaked, the return game still fumbled, and the season ended 5 and 5 — better, but no miracle.

Panacea is the precise word because the town expected one remedy to fix every ill at once. Solution would be too narrow — the passing game did get solved — and savior is melodrama; panacea names the specific fantasy of a single fix for all of it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

cure-all: A cure-all is the plain, homely English word for a remedy claimed to mend every ill — the same sweeping promise a panacea makes. The difference is register: cure-all belongs on a medicine-show poster, while panacea is the formal, usually skeptical word writers reach for to puncture that claim.

elixir: An elixir is a magic potion promising health or long life — a wonder you could pour into a glass. A panacea makes a broader claim in any form: one remedy, policy, or plan said to cure every ill. Elixirs promise magic in a bottle; a panacea promises to mend all ills at once.

magic bullet: A magic bullet is one precise, almost effortless solution aimed at a single stubborn problem — one shot, one cure. A panacea claims far more territory: a single remedy for every ill at once. A magic bullet targets one disease; a panacea supposedly heals the whole ward.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

poison: the opposite promise — a dose that harms whatever it touches

scourge: the ruin or curse of a place, where a panacea would be its rescue

Where it sits · how broad the promised healing is

quick fix → remedy → panacea

quick fix vs. panacea: A quick fix claims the least of all — it patches one symptom for today and may not hold till morning, while a panacea promises to heal every ill at once.

remedy vs. panacea: A remedy honestly treats one particular problem, but it stops short of a panacea, which claims to cure them all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pan-: all (Greek)

Root — acea: cure, remedy (Greek akos, 'cure')

Put it together: Pan- (all) + -acea (from Greek akos, 'cure') = a cure for everything. The Greeks even made her a goddess: Panakeia, daughter of the healer Asklepios. English borrowed the word with its skepticism already attached — from the first, calling something a panacea has hinted that no such thing exists.

Where This Word Comes From: The Greeks made this word a goddess: Panakeia, 'all-healing,' daughter of the healer Asklepios. Her akos ('cure') built no other common English word, so panacea carries it alone. Fittingly, English has used the word with a raised eyebrow from the start — a cure claimed for everything usually cures nothing.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / skeptical

Panacea almost always appears with a wink or a warning — 'is no panacea' is its most common company, because the word names a claim too good to be true. Use it to puncture oversold fixes; for something that honestly targets one problem, remedy or treatment is the straight word.
